title: AI Music Generation, From Prompt to Production: Phlo Young

primary.label: Prompting & LLM Programming
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 45%).

domains.label: Media & Creative
domains.rationale: The workshop's primary focus is on multimodal audio/music AI generation systems including text-to-music, audio-to-music, and voice conversion. The content centers on creative music production using AI tools. The workshop covers prompting for music generation, the generation process, and post-processing via stem extraction and voice conversion. The workshop is explicitly labeled beginner with no musical or coding prerequisites required. An interactive workshop with live demonstrations, hands-on practice, and audience participation. Multiple direct transcript evidence anchors with said_in_transcript grade support the classification.

summary: Phlo Young opens an interactive workshop on AI music generation at the AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco, encouraging audience participation through live polls and a shared notes link. He introduces himself as a songwriter and artist rather than a software engineer, though he uses Python for automation. He shares his experience split-testing the same song under different artist names, finding that cover art, marketing, and targeting caused wildly different performance; one instrumental pen name accumulated roughly 5 million streams. About half the audience has used music generation models. Phlo categorizes AI music into text-to-music, audio-to-music, and style transfer (voice conversion). He demonstrates voice conversion with AI Kanye West and a viral Drake AI song by Ghostwriter that gained approximately 9 million streams in 24 hours before being DMCA'd. He contrasts these with the positive Randy Travis example, where AI helped the artist sing new music after losing his voice. For text-to-music, he plays a Udio-generated meme song and an ElevenLabs viral song. For audio-to-music, he demonstrates Stable Audio and a Suno tool transforming existing sounds into music. Transitioning to hands-on practice, Phlo reveals the RIAA filed a lawsuit against Suno and Udio during the workshop week, alleging training on copyrighted music. He provides shared premier accounts for both platforms and sets up a PVP contest. He attempts to generate a birthday song for audience member Patrick, encountering content filters that block artist names like "Randy Travis." He describes Udio as a "songwriting partner" generating 30-second segments extendable via remix, inpainting, or audio-to-audio upload, and Suno as an "in-house music producer" producing polished top-40-style output. In the final section, he plays multiple versions of Patrick's birthday song and the AI Engineer World's Fair song. He shares a GPT prompt template for generating coherent lyrics before feeding them into music models, and points to the notes page at AI talk.com/music for all prompts and resources. During Q&A, he addresses voice conversion training (minimum 6 seconds of audio needed, can blend multiple voices), recommends RVC for voice cloning, and explains how Rate Your Music labels can be reverse-engineered into prompts. He demonstrates WaveTool for stem extraction by appending "daw" to a song URL, and mentions UVR5 as an open-source local alternative. He defers on ethics, noting he is not a lawyer, and plans a livestream to give away the shared accounts to contest winners. The workshop received 12 song submissions.

sections.title: Workshop Introduction and Audience Interaction
sections.summary: Phlo opens the workshop emphasizing interactivity, shares a notes link, and polls the audience on their experience with AI music tools. About half have used music generation models; some have used Suno or Udio. He asks an audience member for their favorite artist (Miles Davis) and hints at a special demonstration.

sections.title: Phlo's Background and Split-Testing Experience
sections.summary: Phlo introduces himself as a songwriter and artist who uses Python for automation. He describes split-testing the same song under different artist names, finding that marketing and cover art drastically affect performance. One instrumental pen name earned about 5 million streams. He has experimented across R&B, hip-hop, EDM, and country genres.

sections.title: Poll Results and Prompt Engineering Interest
sections.summary: Audience poll submissions show strong interest in prompt techniques and tweaking. Phlo references a 'prompt master' on the Suno/Udio Discord who achieves impressive results with unintuitive prompts for banjo and bagpipe music. He confirms the workshop will include substantial prompting content.

sections.title: Categorizing AI Music and Voice Conversion Demo
sections.summary: Phlo categorizes AI music into text-to-music, audio-to-music, and style transfer (voice conversion). He notes consumers often equate AI music with voice conversion. He plays a video demonstrating AI-generated Kanye West voice covering a popular song, illustrating the implications for the music industry.

sections.title: Voice Conversion Examples: Kanye, Drake, and Randy Travis
sections.summary: Phlo continues the Kanye West voice conversion demo, then plays a viral Drake AI song by Ghostwriter that gained roughly 9 million streams in 24 hours before being DMCA'd. He notes voice conversion tools have improved dramatically over the past year. He contrasts negative public sentiment with the Randy Travis example, where the artist's team used AI to create new music after he lost his voice, receiving overwhelmingly positive response from fans.

sections.title: Text-to-Music: Meme Songs and Full Songs
sections.summary: Phlo introduces text-to-music, subdividing it into meme songs and samples. He plays a BBL Jersey meme song about the Drake-Kendrick Lamar beef, generated by comedian King Wonus using Udio with no prior recording—just text input. He also plays an ElevenLabs text-to-music song about GPUs that went viral on Twitter, demonstrating that complete songs can be generated from text prompts alone.

sections.title: Audio-to-Music Demonstrations
sections.summary: Phlo introduces audio-to-music as the most interesting category for musicians with existing talent. He demonstrates Stable Audio transforming an existing sound into music, noting it was the first tool he saw with this feature publicly available. He also shows a Suno audio-to-music example, highlighting how this approach unlocks new creative possibilities for transforming sounds into music.

sections.title: RIAA Lawsuit and Shared Account Setup
sections.summary: Phlo announces the RIAA filed a complaint against Suno and Udio during the workshop week, alleging the models were trained on copyrighted music. He clarifies he has no affiliation with any company. He provides shared premier accounts for both platforms via business cards with secret codes, sets up a PVP contest where two attendees win account access, and creates a Google form for song submissions. He mentions compiled music model papers are linked on the notes page.

sections.title: Birthday Song Generation and Content Filters
sections.summary: Phlo attempts to generate a birthday song for audience member Patrick, whose 'birthday name' is Randy Travis. The content filter blocks 'Randy Travis' as an artist name. An audience member suggests altering the spelling to bypass filters. Phlo notes both platforms have content filters that block artist names, especially given the lawsuit, and promises to discuss workarounds.

sections.title: Udio vs Suno: Platform Comparison
sections.summary: Phlo describes Udio as a songwriting partner that generates 30-second segments, extendable via remix, extension, inpainting, or the new audio-to-audio upload feature. He urges artists with pre-existing recordings to try uploading their tempo, key, and lyrics into Udio. He describes Suno as an in-house music producer that tends to produce polished top-40-style output, noting Suno has recently improved syllable timing and song structure alignment. He has onboarded about a dozen people recently to understand real use cases.

sections.title: Basic Generation Tutorial
sections.summary: Phlo walks through the basic generation workflow on Udio: navigate to the site, log in, click create, type a prompt, and hit create. He demonstrates by generating a song about the AI Engineer World's Fair in old-school hip hop boom bap style for organizer Benjamin Dy. He notes options for custom lyrics, instrumental-only, and experimental models, and warns about a bug where consecutive generations without refreshing produce unintended extensions.

sections.title: Playing Generated Songs and Prompt Resources
sections.summary: Phlo plays multiple versions of Patrick's birthday song generated on both Udio and Suno, showing lyrics on the Sunno side. He points to the notes section at AI talk.com/music where all prompts, the recording, and a transcript will be available. He shares a GPT prompt template for generating coherent lyrics in ChatGPT before feeding them into music models, noting better results compared to giving a general topic. He mentions official Udio and Suno tips in the notes and warns about GitHub rendering issues with closing brackets.

sections.title: Q&A: Voice Conversion, Ethics, and RVC
sections.summary: Phlo addresses audience questions. On generic voice conversion, he explains a minimum of 6 seconds of audio is needed to train a model, and multiple voices can be blended or a TTS robot voice can be used to avoid copyright. On ethics, he pleads the fifth as a non-lawyer. On best voice cloning tool matching emotional tone, he recommends RVC, noting it can run in the cloud without local hardware. He mentions slides are accessible via the notes page.

sections.title: Rate Your Music, Stem Extraction, and Wrap-Up
sections.summary: Phlo explains how Rate Your Music labels can be reverse-engineered into music model prompts to approximate a specific sound without naming artists. He demonstrates WaveTool stem extraction by appending 'daw' to a Suno song URL, isolating individual instrument and vocal stems with volume control. He mentions UVR5 as a free open-source local alternative requiring decent hardware. He notes 12 contest submissions, plans a livestream to give away accounts, and plays the AI Engineer World's Fair song as an outro before directing attendees to the General Session.
